tasks.short: Greet arriving patients, check identity and details, log their arrival and tell them where to wait.

steps.what: Patient arrives and reports: at the desk today; returning patients scan the QR code at the kiosk after the change
Patient updates contact details in the patient portal before the visit
Medical assistant greets patients arriving and checks their identity
Medical assistant finds the appointment and logs the patient in as arrived
Medical assistant checks and updates contact and insurance details
Medical assistant tells the patient the waiting time and room
Medical assistant handles walk-in patients without an appointment

tasks.design: Configure self check-in in the electronic health record ({OTHER}): returning patients scan the QR code from their appointment confirmation at a kiosk, which sets them as arrived and shows the waiting area. Insurance details are verified the night before through the insurers' check service, and patients update contact details in the patient portal; first visits, ID checks and walk-ins stay at the desk.
tasks.previous_blocker: Check-in happened at the desk because the agenda, insurance check and contact data were desk tasks.
tasks.enabler_now: Health record systems support kiosks and portals, and insurance details can be checked electronically in batch.
tasks.still_hard: Older patients and first visits need the desk; identity checks are a legal duty.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing a patient who looks unwell in the waiting room and calming anxious people.
tasks.altitude: The assistant handles first visits, walk-ins and exceptions; routine arrivals check themselves in.

reach.task: Check in visitors at a front desk
reach.learn: Whether QR check-in from a confirmation message is used by older visitors.

evidence.claim: Clinic kiosks and portals can check patients in from an appointment code and update contact details.
Care providers must verify a patient's identity and citizen service number; details follow national rules.
Health data is special-category data; care use rests on the medical purpose with professional secrecy.

assumptions: Boundary: from the patient's arrival to waiting for the consultation; the consultation is outside.

Input contract: appointment with QR code from the confirmation message, produced by the agenda; insurance status from the insurers' check service the night before; contact details entered by patients in the portal; fallback is the desk.

Scenario: about half of returning patients use the kiosk after a year, about 40% of arrivals; s2 keeps 70 and s3 keeps 60 for desk arrivals and kiosk mismatches; s4 keeps 30 because insurance is checked overnight and patients update contact details in the portal (s1p, customer time); s5 keeps 80.
Patient time is outside the assistant's savings.
unknowns: Whether the practice's record system supports kiosks.
Age profile of the patient list.
research_questions: Which patient groups keep using the desk after kiosks are introduced?

already_counted.description: Assistant resolves kiosk arrivals that do not match an appointment.
Assistant handles insurance check failures from the overnight batch.

incremental.description: Assistant helps patients at the kiosk and resets it when it fails.
Practice manager keeps kiosk texts and confirmation messages current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a practice with many older patients sees few kiosk check-ins, so s2 keeps 90, s3 keeps 85 and s5 keeps 95 (21.5); high: about half of returning patients use the kiosk (35.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Answer telephones, type letters from dictation, complete insurance forms and send them on.

steps.what: Patient states the request to the automated intake on the phone line
Medical assistant answers telephones: results, prescriptions, appointments, questions

loop.input: The caller's spoken request after a message saying they are talking to an automated system.
loop.output: One intent from a fixed list: appointment change, test result request, repeat prescription, other.
loop.check: Any word from a medical-urgency list, or low confidence, routes the call straight to the assistant; intents only open fixed self-service paths.
loop.stop: One re-ask; then the call goes to the assistant.
loop.why_not_simpler: Callers describe their request in their own words; a keypad menu loses many older callers.

steps.what: Medical assistant triages urgent medical calls and passes them to the doctor
Medical assistant types letters from the physician's dictation
Physician checks, corrects and signs the letter
Medical assistant completes insurance and authorisation forms from the record
Medical assistant checks the signed letter before sending: it is the signed version, and the hospital department or patient address in secure messaging
Medical assistant sends signed letters to the hospital or patient
Medical assistant checks the completed form before sending: patient, answers against the record, and the insurer
Medical assistant sends insurance and authorisation forms to the insurer

tasks.design: A phone line with a disclosed automated intake routes routine requests (appointment changes, repeat prescriptions, where to find results in the portal) to fixed self-service paths that give no medical content and anything sounding urgent straight to the assistant. Dictation runs through a CE-marked speech tool inside the health record ({OTHER}), so the physician corrects and signs a draft; insurance forms are pre-filled from record fields, and the assistant checks each signed letter and completed form before sending it once, letters through secure care messaging on the {PARTNER_PORTAL}.
tasks.previous_blocker: Calls were all answered by hand, dictation audio queued for typing, and forms were filled from the record field by field.
tasks.enabler_now: Ambient and dictation tools inside health records are used in Dutch practices, and phone systems take spoken intents with fixed routes.
tasks.still_hard: Telephone triage is a clinical judgement; speech tools make errors that the physician must spot, and patients may hold back when recorded.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing worry in a caller's voice and deciding who needs a doctor today.

ambition.what: Patients who can arrange routine requests outside opening hours without waiting on hold.

tasks.altitude: The assistant spends more phone time on triage and patients who need a person; typing and form-filling shrink.

reach.learn: How much correction a speech draft still needs per letter type.

evidence.claim: A Dutch ambient scribe drafts the consult note for the clinician to approve and is used in many GP practices.
With an ambient scribe, 12 Dutch GPs cut documentation time by 42.7 seconds per consult; total consult time did not change.
A preprint found verified errors in 31.3% of 565 notes from three AI scribes.
A phone bot must tell callers they are speaking to an AI system.
A scribe whose notes feed continued care needs at least MDR Class IIa according to a national regulator's findings.

assumptions: Boundary: from incoming calls and dictations to letters and forms sent; consultations are outside.

Input contract: dictation audio recorded by the physician in the record; record fields for forms kept by clinicians; intent list and urgency words set by the practice manager with the GPs; fallback is answering and typing by hand.
Physician time is outside the assistant's savings.
Telephone triage does not change. The patient's time with the automated intake is shown in s1i. Both checks before sending keep their full time; s6 and s7 keep 30 for the send.
unknowns: Whether the record system has an approved speech tool.
Share of calls that are routine.
research_questions: How often do callers routed to self-service call back for the same request?

already_counted.description: Assistant checks formatting and addresses on speech-drafted letters.
Assistant checks pre-filled form fields against the record.

incremental.description: Assistant calls back patients whose automated request failed.
Practice manager keeps intents, urgency words and form templates current.

approvals.approved_version: The letter exactly as signed by the physician in s4 and checked by the assistant in s5b, sent once by secure care messaging to the named hospital department or patient; any edit needs a new signature and check.
The insurance or authorisation form with its answers exactly as checked by the assistant in s6c, sent once to the patient's insurer; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: most callers want to speak to a person and speech drafts have many errors, so s1 keeps 90 and s3 keeps 60 (28.8); high: as designed (46.4).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Prepare repeat prescriptions for the doctor to authorize, send them to pharmacies and answer pharmacy questions.

steps.what: Patient requests refills through the line, portal or pharmacy
Medical assistant finds the medication and checks it is a chronic repeat
Medical assistant checks the last control visit and due lab tests
Medical assistant prepares the refill prescription for the doctor
General practitioner reviews the prepared refill: medicine, dose, quantity, the repeat policy flags and the patient's pharmacy
General practitioner signs and sends the reviewed e-prescription to the patient's pharmacy
Medical assistant sends the e-prescription to the patient's pharmacy; after the change the GP's signing sends it
Medical assistant answers pharmacies' questions on dosage or interactions, consulting the doctor

tasks.design: Patients pick the medicine from their own active repeat list in the patient portal; fixed rules in the health record ({OTHER}) check chronic status, last control date and due lab tests against the GP's repeat policy per medicine, and put a prepared prescription in the GP's authorisation queue or flag it for the assistant. The GP reviews each prepared refill and signs and sends the e-prescription once to the patient's pharmacy.
tasks.previous_blocker: Repeat requests came in by phone and were checked record by record because repeat policies were not stored as fields.
tasks.enabler_now: Health records hold medication lists and dates, portals take structured requests, and e-prescribing to pharmacies is standard.
tasks.still_hard: Repeat policies per medicine must be set and kept by GPs; dosage and interaction questions need clinical knowledge.
tasks.human_edge: Spotting the patient who should not just get another refill and making sure the doctor sees them.

ambition.what: Every repeat checked against control and lab dates, so overdue monitoring is caught at each refill.

tasks.altitude: The assistant handles flagged requests and pharmacy questions; the GP authorises from a clean queue.

reach.task: Request refill authorisation from the practice
reach.learn: Which missing details cause most pharmacy calls.

evidence.claim: Health record systems and patient portals can take structured repeat requests and send e-prescriptions.
Prescribing is reserved to the doctor; the assistant prepares and the doctor authorises under national rules.
Software that supports clinical decisions may fall under medical device rules depending on its purpose; fixed rules mirroring the practice's own policy, with the doctor deciding, are the design here.
The medical record is kept 20 years and shared only with consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from the refill request to the e-prescription sent and questions answered; dispensing is outside.

Input contract: active repeat list per patient and repeat policy per medicine (control interval, lab tests), set by the GPs in the health record; request entered by the patient in the portal; fallback is the phone line.
GP time is outside the assistant's savings; pharmacy staff time is outside too.
unknowns: Whether the record system stores repeat policies as fields.
Share of refill requests via the portal.
research_questions: How often are refills issued while monitoring is overdue today?

already_counted.description: Assistant reviews requests the rules could not match to an active repeat.
Assistant reviews refills flagged for overdue control or lab tests.
Assistant checks the auto-prepared prescription before it goes to the GP.

incremental.description: Assistant helps patients whose portal request fails.
GPs set and update repeat policies per medicine.

approvals.approved_version: The prescription with medicine, dose and quantity exactly as reviewed by the GP in s5, signed and sent once to the patient's pharmacy; any change needs a new review.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few patients use the portal and many repeats lack a policy, so the rules match fewer requests and s2 and s3 keep 60 (42.7); high: as designed (55.9).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Schedule appointments for patients with the right professional and slot, and handle changes and reminders.

steps.what: Patient asks for an appointment: by phone or at the desk today, by booking online for routine types after the change
Medical assistant asks the reason and urgency to choose professional and slot length
Medical assistant searches the agenda for a suitable free slot for patients
Medical assistant schedules the appointment and confirms date and time
Medical assistant reschedules cancellations and fills gaps from the waiting list: by phone today; after the change picks the waiting-list patients for each freed slot
Medical assistant checks each slot offer: slot, professional, appointment type and the waiting-list patients it goes to
Medical assistant releases the checked slot offers by text message
Medical assistant sends reminders and calls patients who did not show: by phone today; after the change calls no-shows only
Medical assistant checks the next day's reminders: patient, date, time, professional and mobile number
Medical assistant releases the checked reminders by text message

tasks.design: Configure online booking in the health record ({OTHER}) for routine appointment types with fixed reasons and slot lengths; a reason that contains a red-flag word is not bookable and asks the patient to call. Patients see their online booking confirmed on screen. The assistant checks the next day's reminders and releases them once by text message, and checks offers of freed slots to waiting-list patients before releasing them.
tasks.previous_blocker: Practices kept booking by phone to control urgency and slot lengths.
tasks.enabler_now: Health record agendas support online booking per appointment type, reminders and waiting lists.
tasks.still_hard: Choosing urgency and the right professional needs the assistant for anything but routine; some patients will not book online.
tasks.human_edge: Judging over the phone who needs to be seen today and fitting in the patient who needs it most.

ambition.what: Working patients who book routine appointments in the evening instead of calling during work hours.

tasks.altitude: The assistant books the patients who need judgement and lets routine bookings run themselves.

reach.learn: Whether recall bookings move online faster than ad-hoc ones.

evidence.claim: Online booking, a phone bot of fixed menus with a bounded intent step, and medical questions routed to the assistant cover scheduling calls.
Appointment data with a reason is health data under GDPR.

assumptions: Boundary: from the request to the appointment kept or rescheduled; the consultation is outside.

Input contract: bookable appointment types with reasons, professional and slot length, and the red-flag word list, set by the practice manager with the GPs; waiting list kept in the agenda; fallback is the phone.

Scenario: about 40% of routine bookings move online in the first year. The offer and reminder checks and releases keep their full time; s5 keeps 50 for choosing waiting-list patients and phone rescheduling; s6 keeps 30 for calling no-shows.
Patient time is outside the assistant's savings.
unknowns: Share of appointments that are routine and bookable online.
research_questions: Do automated reminders reduce no-shows for this patient list?

already_counted.description: Assistant calls back patients whose online reason hit a red-flag word.

incremental.description: Assistant fixes double or wrong-type online bookings.
Practice manager keeps appointment types and the red-flag list current.

approvals.approved_version: Each slot offer with slot, professional and appointment type exactly as checked by the assistant in s5b, sent once by text message to the named waiting-list patients; any change needs a new check.

The next day's reminders with date, time and professional exactly as checked by the assistant in s6b, sent once by text message to each patient's mobile number in the agenda; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: only a fifth of patients book online, so phone scheduling stays most of the work; s2 keeps 85, s3 keeps 80 and s4 keeps 70 (26.6); high: about 40% online as assumed (41.3).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The assistant keeps triage, the desk for those who need it and pharmacy questions; routine check-ins, bookings, refills and typing shift to systems.
skills_to_grow: Handling the exceptions automated flows hand over
Checking speech drafts and pre-filled forms
Explaining portals and self-service to patients
role.ambitious_version: An assistant who spends most of the day on triage and patients who need a person, while routine requests run through checked self-service.
